I read about two hundred board packs a year, and I can tell you what I do in the first ninety seconds. I look for the sentences that still have a person in them. Not because I want to know who did it, but because those are the sentences somebody fought over. Everything that was uncontroversial has already been flattened into the impersonal form: the accounts were audited, churn is measured this way, the numbers are shown against the benchmark. Nobody argues about those, so nobody is standing behind them. Then, in the middle of all that, you find one line that says my team delivered this, or the commercial director committed to that, and there is your fault line. That is where the disagreement lives. It is the only reliable way I know to find the real risk in a document that has been written by eight people who all wanted it to look calm.

Founders send us numbers and they think the number is the message. It is not. The definition is the message. If you tell me churn is eight percent, I have learned almost nothing, because I do not yet know what was counted. Eight percent of clients, or eight percent of revenue? Measured monthly and multiplied, or measured over the full year? Does a client who reduced their contract by half count as churn, or as nothing at all? Three companies can report the same eight percent and mean three different businesses. So write the definition into the sentence, every time, in the impersonal form: churn is measured on client count, not on revenue, over trailing twelve months. It takes eleven words. And when the numbers have been audited, say who audited them, because the name is doing work that the sentence cannot do without it.
